The transition from Coptic to Arabic as the dominant language in Egypt was a gradual process spanning several centuries, with different milestones at different times. According to a peer-reviewed academic source, the process began in earnest in the late ninth century, and by the end of the twelfth century Arabic had become the main written language of the Church; by the thirteenth century, Coptic was already a classical language known only to scholars [d5]. Flashcard sources based on historical coursework identify the fourteenth century C.E. — following the conversion of most rural Coptic Christians — as when Arabic overtook Coptic as the language most used in Egypt [d1][d2]. A WordPress resource on Coptic history adds that by the fifteenth century Coptic had ceased entirely to be a spoken language, though it continued in liturgical use [d10]. By around 900 CE, even Coptic speakers were already using Arabic legal records, indicating Arabic's growing dominance well before the fourteenth century [d9], and Wikipedia confirms that by the Mameluke era the Arabization of the Egyptian populace had fully taken place [d6].
